  "text": "The library charged no fines for overdue books.

Instead, you returned a memory.

A day late cost something small: a breakfast, a bus ride. After a year, people brought wedding photographs to help them remember what they had paid.

My father died with a library book beneath his pillow.

It was thirty-six years overdue.

I took it back on Tuesday.

The librarian opened the cover, then closed it carefully.

“You aren’t responsible for his debts.”

“I know.”

“Did you read it?”

The pages were blank. I told her so.

She turned the book toward the window. In the thin September light, handwriting appeared.

My first tooth. The afternoon I learned to swim. A terrible joke I told every Christmas.

“He borrowed extra time,” she said.

I remembered hospitals. Then, suddenly, no hospitals. My father making pancakes, burning every third one.

“How much?”

“Everything you remember about him.”

Outside, someone was teaching a child to ride a bicycle. The child kept shouting, Don’t let go.

“And if I don’t pay?”

“Nothing. The debt ends here.”

I put my hand on the book.

There were things I wanted gone. Our last argument. His frightened face when he forgot my name.

There were pancakes.

“Can I keep it?”

She fetched a stamp from a drawer.

WITHDRAWN, it said.

On the bus home, I opened the book again. The writing had vanished except for one line near the back, pressed so hard into the paper I could feel it with my thumb.

Stayed for her.

At home I set it beside the stove, well away from the burner, and made myself something to eat."
